findings.title: Async callback rejection lets writes escape the transaction
findings.body: The callback is invoked before the transaction helper detects that it returned a Promise. An async callback that writes after `await` can therefore be rolled back and rejected, then continue after `#transactionDatabase` has been cleared; a later `appendFact` can open and commit a separate transaction. The in-memory owner has the analogous post-await escape. Reject async callbacks before invoking them, rather than only inspecting the returned Promise after side effects may already have started.

findings.title: DELETE can report applied for a conflicting duplicate invalidation
findings.body: `invalidateFact` treats any existing row with the same invalidation ID as a successful duplicate without verifying its fact, verification status, or invalidation time. For example, a previously persisted candidate-status invalidation with the same predictable ID is not accepted, yet `requirePersisted` accepts the duplicate result and DELETE returns `applied` while the target remains active. A conflicting row for another target has the same problem. Verify that the deduplicated invalidation is accepted and applies to the requested target, or reject conflicting IDs.

overall_explanation: The synchronous SQLite savepoint and in-memory rollback paths are largely coherent, but two atomicity-contract gaps remain. Async callbacks are rejected only after invocation, allowing post-await writes to escape the intended transaction. DELETE also trusts a deduplicated invalidation result without checking that the persisted row is an accepted invalidation for the requested target, so it can report `applied` while the deletion effect is absent.
